newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-N.Zealand wool industry hoping to catch boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-N.Zealand wool industry hoping to catch boom.

text.p: Surging wool prices in Australia and other big producers have by-passed New Zealand farmers but industry commentators on Tuesday said they saw a gradual improvement in the 1997/98 season starting next month.

"In the immediate future, we see continuation of the same," Patrick Conway, Wools of New Zealand manager of economics and market information, told Reuters. "We expect longer-term things will improve, especially as Australian stocks are run down."

"I think there will be a gradual improvement. Don't look for any starry-eyed stuff, but a slow improvement over the next two years," said John Dawson, General Manager of exporter New Zealand Wool Services International.
Lower production and a gradual improvement in key markets in China and Western Europe would underpin firmer prices, he said.
New Zealand produces mainly coarse wools, used in carpets and furnishings, while Australia grows predominantly fine wools used in apparel.
While prices for fine wools have recently gone northward, the price for coarse wools have largely stagnated, particularly when measured against the muscular New Zealand dollar.
Historically, coarse and fine wools prices have seldom diverged for long.
"Over the long-term they correlate pretty well. We'd expect to see some upturn in strong wool prices," Conway said.
New Zealand has the world's fourth biggest flock, ranks second in fibre production and grows a quarter of coarse wool.
The kiwi dollar's climb against the yen and European currencies in the past two years is partly behind poor returns.
The New Zealand market indicator, now at NZ$4.50/kg clean from $4.56 a year ago, has slumped 28 percent from a peak of $6.28 in March 1995.
China, which bought 37 percent of New Zealand's clip in 1995/96 is the main reason for weakness in the prices here.

"The situation in China has to be a major dampener on our market at the moment. We're still exporting there only about 50 percent of the volumes that we were exporting in the same month in 1996," Conway said.

The blame is put on a combination of factors -- slowdown of Chinese economy, excess stocks, quality problems, cowboy traders in a newly opened market, and financial problems -- none of which appear to have upset the Australian industry.
Dawson said the difference is due to fashion.
Australian wool goes into fine worsted fabrics currently in demand in Europe while carpet sales are still languishing.
Dawson added New Zealand farmers had failed to read the market well. "There's too much wool in the coarse category and one would have to say that the market for that type of wool is limited."
Wool has also lost market share to man-made fibres such as polypropolene in the carpet market.
However, New Zealand farmers are getting good prices for lamb and mutton so overproduction of coarse wool is inevitable.
The sale of the last bale in New Zealand's stockpile in December 1995 and the decline in sheep numbers from a high of 72 million to 48 million ought point to lower production.
But a good 1996/97 growing season and higher yield per animal has seen production steady at 200,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
A 2.5 percent decline is forecast for 1997/98.
Exporter Kai Tovgaard, Vice President of the Wool Exporters Council, said many processors had bought wool forward for three months and he expects a pick-up in prices early next season.
"There are real prospects of better prices next season. Demand hasn't been very good for the last 12 months but I see us turning the corner simply because wool is cheap," he said.
"Fine wools will be a lot better next season. Coarser wools will not be as good relatively, but prices will still go up."
-- Wellington newsroom, 64 4 4734 746
